claims.text: The alloy has a multiphase eutectic microstructure with distinct phases and interphase boundaries.
The interphase boundaries are chemically or electrochemically active.
Tailored heat treatment or chemical passivation can render the interphase boundaries electrochemically inert.
Interphase boundaries control local protective-oxide integrity.
Interphase boundaries control galvanic coupling between the constituent phases.
Sliding wear ruptures protective oxide films at interphase boundaries.
Oxide-film rupture exposes dissimilar phases having different electrochemical potentials.
The exposed dissimilar phases form local galvanic cells.
Local galvanic cells accelerate corrosion in worn regions.
Wear-induced oxide disruption and galvanic corrosion directly produce synergistic wear-corrosion degradation.
The standard alloy with active boundaries will have greater total degradation than a matched alloy with passivated boundaries.
The standard alloy will have greater wear-induced material loss than the passivated-boundary baseline.
The standard alloy will have a higher corrosion rate than the passivated-boundary baseline.
Wear-corrosion coupling enhances both mechanical material removal and corrosion attack.
Passivating the interphase boundaries minimizes galvanic interactions.
The controlled comparison uses the same alloy in active-boundary and passivated-boundary states under identical thermal, mechanical, and chemical loading.
Total mass loss, wear-track geometry, electrochemical response, oxide integrity, and microscopic evidence of galvanic coupling are measurable test outputs.
Failure of boundary passivation to produce a statistically significant reduction in both total degradation and localized wear-corrosion damage would falsify the hypothesis.
